property_summary: For every caller, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some callers — so owner() should never be zero for the reference but can be zero in the mutant.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the non-zero address set at construction (the deployer), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some callers, so the property is: owner() != address(0) always holds on the reference but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For all callers, the correct contract's owner() returns the deployer address (non-zero) while the mutant returns zero for some callers; therefore the invariant is that calling owner() from any caller yields the same non-zero address (the deployer), and the mutant breaks this by returning address(0) for some caller inputs.
For every caller, the reference contract's owner() call returns a non-zero address (the stored owner); the mutant returns address(0) for some callers, violating this invariant.

For every caller the reference contract's owner() returns the same non-changing stored owner address (the deployer) while the mutant sometimes returns address(0); thus the general rule: owner() never returns the zero address for any caller on the reference, whereas the mutant violates this for some caller address.

For any caller address, the reference contract's owner() always returns the stored owner (the deployer), whereas the mutant returns msg.sender (i.e. caller) — so the general rule: owner() == deployer for all callers; the mutant breaks this for any caller != deployer.

For all callers, the deployed contract's owner() always returns the original deployer address; the mutant that returns msg.sender violates this because owner() will return the caller when the caller != deployer.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the deploying owner address (the stored owner); the mutant that returns msg.sender will return a different address whenever a caller other than the deployer calls owner(), violating that rule.

For every caller, C.owner() returns the original deployer address (the stored owner); the mutant returning msg.sender will return a different address for some caller (any caller != deployer), breaking this rule.

For every caller, C.owner() returns the stored deployer-owner address; the mutant that returns msg.sender will return a different address when called by any account other than the deployer, breaking this invariant.

For all inputs, the reference contract's owner() getter returns the stored owner (the deployer/transferable owner), whereas the mutant returns address(this) causing owner() to differ from the stored owner for some inputs (e.g., when stored owner != address(this)).

For every contract state, owner() must return the stored owner address (_owner) (so owner() == address(this) only when the stored owner equals the contract address); the mutant always returns address(this) so it violates the equality for any stored owner != address(this).

For every deployment and state, C.owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer) — the mutant returns address(this) instead, so for any state where the stored owner != address(this) the mutant violates this rule.

For every state, the contract's owner() getter returns the stored owner address (the deployer/assigned owner); the mutant that returns address(this) will differ whenever the stored owner is not the contract address.

For all inputs, the reference C.owner() call returns the stored owner address (initially the deployer/address(this) at construction and after transfers), whereas the mutant that always returns address(this) will differ whenever the stored owner is any address other than the contract itself — we assert that after transferring ownership to a fuzzed address, owner() equals that address (holds in reference, broken in mutant).

For all non-zero newOwner addresses, transferOwnership succeeds and sets owner to that address; the mutant which allows zero-address will cause a call with newOwner = address(0) to succeed and set owner to zero, violating the rule that owner is never set to the zero address by transferOwnership.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract either reverts when newOwner == address(0) or results in owner() == newOwner for any input; the mutant removes the require check so transferOwnership(address(0)) succeeds and sets owner() == address(0), violating the invariant.

For all addresses x, calling transferOwnership(x) on the correct contract either reverts if x == address(0) or results in owner() == x; the mutant removes the check and allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed leaving owner() == address(0), violating this rule.

For all addresses newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) either reverts (when newOwner == address(0)) or results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant removes the require check and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and set owner() == address(0), violating the rule.

For all addresses newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract either reverts when newOwner == address(0) (so owner() is never set to zero) or results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant removes the require and therefore allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and set owner() == address(0), violating that owner() is never set to the zero address by transferOwnership.

Calling transferOwnership(newOwner) should always succeed (i.e., not revert) when newOwner is equal to the current owner or any non-zero address; the mutant incorrectly reverts when newOwner == current owner.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner never reverts for any address (including the current owner) in the reference contract; the mutant adds a require that reverts when newOwner == owner(), so it will sometimes revert.

For any address newOwner, when called by the current owner transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference contract always succeeds (does not revert) — the mutant adds a check disallowing transferring to the same owner which makes the call revert when newOwner == owner(), so some inputs cause a revert there.

For any address newOwner, when the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the reference contract never reverts (call always succeeds); the mutant wrongly reverts when newOwner == owner() causing at least one input to fail.

When the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) the reference contract never reverts (call always succeeds) for any newOwner address, but the mutant adds a check that causes a revert when newOwner == owner(), so some inputs will make transferOwnership revert on the mutant while the reference always succeeds.

For any non-zero address passed to setOperator by the owner, the contract's operator state becomes exactly that address; the mutant incorrectly sets operator to address(0) so this property will be violated for some fuzzed non-zero addresses.

For any non-zero address provided by the owner to setOperator, the reference contract sets operator to that address, whereas the mutant sets operator to address(0), so there exists some non-zero address input where operator() differs.

For any nonzero address a passed to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract sets operator() == a, whereas the mutant sets operator() == address(0) for some such a (so there exists an owner-invoked call where operator() differs).

For every address newOp passed to setOperator by the contract owner, the reference contract sets operator() == newOp; the mutant instead sets operator() == address(0) for some non-zero newOp, so there exist inputs (non-zero newOp) where operator() differs.

For every address newOp passed to setOperator by the owner, the reference contract sets operator() == newOp; the mutant instead sets operator() == address(0) for some non-zero newOp, so there exist inputs where operator() differs.

For any caller X calling setOperator(newOp) as the owner, the contract's operator becomes exactly the provided newOp; the mutant sets operator to the caller instead, breaking this property for inputs where caller != newOp.

For any owner caller and any address x, after calling setOperator(x) as the owner the contract's operator equals the provided x; the mutant assigns msg.sender instead, so when owner != x the mutant's operator differs.

For every owner caller and any address newOp, calling setOperator(newOp) sets c.operator() equal to the provided newOp; the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender, so when the owner (caller) != newOp the mutant will violate this rule.

For any address newOp and when the caller is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOp) sets c.operator() == newOp; the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender and therefore violates this when owner != newOp.

For any address newOp and when the caller is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOp) sets c.operator() equal to the provided newOp; the mutant instead sets operator to msg.sender and thus will differ whenever owner != newOp.

For any caller address X, if X is the contract owner then calling setOperator(X) succeeds and sets operator to X; the mutant makes owner-only checks effectively require owner==address(0) so a non-zero owner cannot call setOperator and the call will revert (operator remains unchanged) for some owner X.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(...) on the correct contract succeeds and updates operator to the provided address; the mutant makes owner-only calls fail when owner != address(0), so some owner callers cannot update operator.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOp) on the correct contract always succeeds and sets operator() == newOp; the mutant makes owner-only checks depend on owner()==address(0) causing some owner callers to be unable to call setOperator (call reverts) and thus operator() may not equal newOp for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOperator) always succeeds on the reference contract and sets operator()==newOperator; the mutant makes owner-only calls require owner()==address(0) and thus some owner callers cannot successfully call setOperator, so operator() may remain unchanged (call reverts) for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling setOperator(newOp) always succeeds on the reference C and sets operator() == newOp; the mutant makes onlyOwner require owner()==address(0) and thus some owner callers will have their setOperator call revert (operator() will not be updated), so the universal rule is violated for some inputs.

For any input address x, calling setRewardsRecipient(x) on the correct contract stores x in rewardsRecipient (and leaves operator unchanged unless x equals operator), whereas the mutant mistakenly writes x into operator instead, so rewardsRecipient remains different; the test fuzzes the input address and asserts that rewardsRecipient equals the provided address after the call.

For any address X passed to setRewardsRecipient, the correct contract stores X in rewardsRecipient (so rewardsRecipient() == X after the call); the mutant instead writes X into operator (so rewardsRecipient() != X for inputs where operator would change), breaking that rule for some X.

For every input address a, calling setRewardsRecipient(a) on the correct contract stores a into rewardsRecipient (rewardsRecipient() == a); the mutant instead writes a into operator, so for some a the equality rewardsRecipient() == a fails.

For every input address x, after calling setRewardsRecipient(x) the correct contract stores x in rewardsRecipient (rewardsRecipient() == x); the mutant instead writes x into operator, so there exist inputs where rewardsRecipient() != x and the property is violated.

For every address a, calling setRewardsRecipient(a) on the correct contract stores a into rewardsRecipient (rewardsRecipient() == a); the mutant writes to operator instead so there exist inputs a for which rewardsRecipient() != a and the property is violated.

For any input address arg, calling setRewardsRecipient(arg) sets c.rewardsRecipient() equal to the provided arg; the mutant that always sets it to zero breaks this by making rewardsRecipient() == address(0) for some non-zero arg.

For any non-zero address input x, calling setRewardsRecipient(x) results in c.rewardsRecipient() == x (reference); the mutant that ignores the argument and sets rewardsRecipient to address(0) violates this for some non-zero x.

For every address a passed to setRewardsRecipient(a) by the owner, the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == a, whereas the mutant that unconditionally sets rewardsRecipient = address(0) will cause rewardsRecipient != a for some non-zero a.

For any address a passed by the owner to setRewardsRecipient(a), the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == a; the mutant that ignores the argument and sets rewardsRecipient = address(0) will make rewardsRecipient != a for some non-zero a.

For every address a provided by the owner to setRewardsRecipient(a), the reference contract stores rewardsRecipient == a; the mutant that unconditionally sets rewardsRecipient = address(0) will violate this rule for some non-zero a.

Calling setRewardsRecipient(x) by the owner always sets c.rewardsRecipient() equal to the provided argument x (for every input); the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so for some x (when owner != x) the stored rewardsRecipient will differ and the property is violated.

For any address chosen as the rewards recipient, when the contract owner calls setRewardsRecipient(addr) the stored rewardsRecipient equals the provided addr (the mutant incorrectly stores msg.sender and thus can differ when owner != addr).

For any address recipient and any caller who is the contract owner, after calling setRewardsRecipient(recipient) the contract's rewardsRecipient getter equals the provided recipient; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will violate this whenever the owner is not equal to the provided recipient (some fuzzed inputs).

For any address chosen as newRecipient and when the contract owner calls setRewardsRecipient(newRecipient), the contract's rewardsRecipient getter equals the provided newRecipient; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead will store the caller (owner) so when newRecipient != owner the property is violated.

For every address X and when the contract owner calls setRewardsRecipient(X), the contract's rewardsRecipient getter equals X; the mutant that sets rewardsRecipient = msg.sender violates this whenever X != owner (so some fuzzed X will differ).

Rule: Only the owner (owner()) can successfully call setRewardsRecipient(address) when called directly (msg.sender); the mutant using tx.origin allows a different caller via tx.origin mismatches, so there exists a caller address that can set rewardsRecipient on the mutant but not on the reference.

For every caller address X and target recipient R, in the correct contract only the true owner (owner() == msg.sender) can call setRewardsRecipient(R) successfully; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin allows a contract caller (msg.sender != tx.origin) to succeed when tx.origin equals the owner, breaking that invariant for some inputs.

For all callers and recipient addresses, only a direct call from the account equal to owner() (i.e. msg.sender == owner()) can successfully execute setRewardsRecipient on the correct contract; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead can be made to succeed when a contract (caller) forwards a call initiated by the owner (tx.origin == owner but msg.sender != owner), thus violating the invariant for some inputs.

For all caller and recipient addresses, in the reference contract only a transaction whose msg.sender equals owner() can successfully call setRewardsRecipient (so the call reverts for any msg.sender != owner()); the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead allows a contract to forward an owner-originated transaction (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to succeed, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every caller address and recipient, in the reference contract only a call whose msg.sender equals owner() can successfully set rewardsRecipient; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead allows a contract to forward an owner-originated transaction (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to set rewardsRecipient, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller address, calling setRewardsRecipient on the correct contract only succeeds when the caller is the owner (so rewardsRecipient can only be changed by the owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check allowing non-owners to change rewardsRecipient, violating this invariant for some caller address.
For all caller addresses, only the contract owner can successfully change rewardsRecipient; the mutant removing onlyOwner allows some non-owner caller to change rewardsRecipient, violating this rule.
